chunks: "The core idea is that you never measure current directly, you convert it to a voltage. There are really three families.
First, resistive: put a small sense resistor, a shunt, in series with the load and measure the voltage across it, V equals IR .
Usually I'd amplify that with a current sense amplifier and feed it to an ADC.
It's cheap, accurate, and works from DC up to high frequency, but it burns I to the 2R power and has no isolation. Second, use a resistance that's already there.
A MOSFET's on-resistance, V DS equals I times R DS(on) , or an inductor's DC resistance with an RC filter.
No extra loss, but the accuracy is poor because those resistances drift with temperature and vary part to part.
Third, magnetic: Hall-effect sensors for DC and AC, current transformers or Rogowski coils for AC only.
They give isolation and almost no insertion loss, but they cost more, take space, and drift in offset. So my default for a low-voltage board is a shunt plus CSA.
I'd go to Hall or a transformer when I need isolation or have hundreds of amps."
